title: B-25J Mitchell (pilot)

sources.title: IL-2 Sturmovik 1946 Aircraft Guide (instrument panel numbers, B-25J-1NA)
JoyPro cockpit catalog (panels, items and grip functions of the variant)

intro: The B-25 Mitchell is an American twin-engine medium bomber of the Second World War. The pilot (left) and the co-pilot sit side by side with control wheels, and between them a pedestal carries the paired throttle, propeller and mixture levers. The bombardier sits in the glazed nose; gunship versions with a solid nose fired fixed guns from the pilot's wheel. The instrument panel numbers follow the IL-2 1946 Aircraft Guide; the pedestal and side panels follow the general B-25 layout, and the wheel button is inferred.

areas.name: Instrument panel
areas.text: The shared panel in front of both pilots.

panels.name: Instrument panel
panels.text: The panel shared by the two pilots: the flight instruments on the pilot's (left) side, the engine gauges in the middle, and the gear and flap indicators on the right.
panels.context: The numbers follow the IL-2 1946 Aircraft Guide for the B-25J; most engine gauges show both engines at once with two needles.

controls.name: Magnetic compass
controls.text: A simple magnetic compass on the windshield frame. It shows the heading without electricity.
controls.context: It is outside the guide's picture; the pilots use it to check the other compasses.

controls.name: Pilot's Direction Indicator
controls.text: An instrument that shows the pilot which way to steer during the bomb run; the bombardier in the nose sends the corrections to it.
controls.context: The guide lists it twice (numbers 2 and 24); this entry covers both.

controls.name: Radio Compass
controls.text: This instrument points to a radio station the radio compass is tuned to (ADF, a radio beacon receiver).
controls.context: The pilots use it to fly towards or away from a station, for example to find home.

controls.name: Compass
controls.text: A compass that shows the heading, the direction the nose points.
controls.context: The guide lists a compass at numbers 4 and 13; this entry covers both.

controls.name: Manifold Pressure (Engine #1 & #2)
controls.text: This gauge shows the manifold pressure, how hard air is pushed into each engine, which is a measure of the engine's power. It has two needles, one for each engine.
controls.context: The pilot sets the power with the throttles while watching this gauge.

controls.name: RPM Indicator (Engine #1 & #2)
controls.text: This gauge shows how fast each engine and its propeller turn (RPM). It has two needles, one for each engine.
controls.context: The propeller levers set the RPM; the pilot checks it here.

controls.name: Suction Gauge
controls.text: This gauge shows the suction (vacuum) that drives the gyro instruments, such as the artificial horizon and the direction indicator.
controls.context: Without enough suction those instruments slowly become wrong.

controls.name: Fuel Pressure (Engine #1 & #2)
controls.text: This gauge shows the pressure of the fuel going to each engine. It has two needles, one for each engine.
controls.context: Low fuel pressure can mean a pump problem or an empty tank.

controls.name: Oil Pressure (Engine #1 & #2)
controls.text: This gauge shows the oil pressure of each engine. It has two needles, one for each engine.
controls.context: Losing oil pressure means the engine is in danger and may have to be shut down.

controls.name: Fuel Level gauges (front, rear, auxiliary)
controls.text: Three gauges that show how much fuel is in the front tanks, the rear tanks and the auxiliary tanks.
controls.context: The crew watches them to plan the flight and to switch tanks.

controls.name: Landing Gear Position Indicator
controls.text: Lamps that show whether the wheels are up or down and locked.
controls.context: The pilot checks them before every landing.

controls.name: Airspeed Indicator
controls.text: This dial shows how fast the aircraft moves through the air, and also the Mach number (the speed as a multiple of the speed of sound).
controls.context: The pilot watches it closely on take-off and landing, where the right speed matters most.

controls.name: Artificial Horizon
controls.text: This instrument shows whether the nose points up or down and whether the wings are level, like a picture of the horizon (artificial horizon). It is driven by a gyro.
controls.context: It is the most important instrument for flying in cloud or at night, when the real horizon cannot be seen.

controls.name: Clock
controls.text: A clock on the panel that shows the time of day.
controls.context: The crew uses it to time the legs of the route.

controls.name: Carburetor Air Temperature (Engine #1 & #2)
controls.text: This gauge shows the temperature of the air going into each engine's carburetor. It has two needles, one for each engine.
controls.context: If it gets too cold, ice can form in the carburetor; the carburetor air levers then add warm air.

controls.name: Oil Temperature (Engine #1 & #2)
controls.text: This gauge shows how hot the oil of each engine is. It has two needles, one for each engine.
controls.context: The pilots wait for warm oil before take-off and watch for overheating in a long climb.

controls.name: Flap Position Indicator
controls.text: This gauge shows how far the flaps are down.
controls.context: The pilot checks it when setting the flaps for take-off and landing.

controls.name: Hydraulic Pressure
controls.text: This gauge shows the pressure of the hydraulics, oil under high pressure that moves the gear, flaps and bomb bay doors.
controls.context: Without hydraulic pressure those parts cannot move normally.

controls.name: Altimeter
controls.text: The height gauge. It shows how high the aircraft is; the pilot sets the local air pressure on it so it reads right.
controls.context: The pilot uses it to hold a height and to know how far above the ground he is when landing.

controls.name: Turn & Bank Indicator
controls.text: This instrument shows how fast the aircraft turns (a needle) and whether it slips sideways (a ball).
controls.context: Keeping the ball in the middle with the rudder makes a clean turn.

controls.name: Variometer
controls.text: This dial shows whether the aircraft climbs or sinks, and how fast.
controls.context: The pilot uses it to hold level flight and to make a smooth, steady descent for landing.

controls.name: Cylinder Head Temperature (Engine #1 & #2)
controls.text: This gauge shows how hot the cylinders of each engine are. It has two needles, one for each engine.
controls.context: The pilots open the cowl flaps or reduce power if the engines run too hot.

controls.name: Free Air Temperature
controls.text: This gauge shows the temperature of the air outside.
controls.context: It helps the crew judge the risk of ice on the wings and in the carburetors.

controls.name: Landing and navigation light switches
controls.text: Switches for the landing lights and the navigation lights (the coloured lights on the wing tips and tail).
controls.context: They are used for night flying and landing.

controls.name: Brake Pressure
controls.text: This gauge shows the pressure available for the wheel brakes.
controls.context: The pilot checks it before taxiing and landing.

panels.name: Control pedestal
panels.text: The pedestal between the two pilots, with the engine levers and the trim controls. The engine levers and trims are explained under the throttle quadrant below; here are the other two.
panels.context: Either pilot can reach the pedestal, so the co-pilot can help with the engines.

controls.name: Carburetor air levers
controls.text: Levers that choose cold or warm air for the carburetors.
controls.context: Warm air stops ice from forming in the carburetors in cold, damp weather.

controls.name: Friction locks
controls.text: Knobs that make the engine levers stiffer, so they stay where they are set.
controls.context: Without friction the levers could creep back on a long flight.

panels.name: Pilot's side panel
panels.text: The panel at the pilot's left with the ignition, the electrics, the engine starters and the radio.
panels.context: These are the switches of the engine start.

controls.name: Ignition switches

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: No sparks; the engine cannot run.

controls.text: Switches for the magnetos, the small generators that make the sparks for each engine; there are two per engine for safety.
controls.context: The pilot checks each magneto alone before take-off and flies on BOTH.

controls.name: Battery and generator switches
controls.text: Switches for the battery (stores electricity) and the generators (make electricity while the engines run).
controls.context: The battery comes first for the engine start; the generators take over afterwards.

controls.name: Starter and mesh switches
controls.text: Switches for starting the engines: first the starter is spun up, then the 'mesh' switch connects it to the engine to turn it over.
controls.context: The pilot starts one engine after the other.

controls.name: Radio control box
controls.text: The control box of the radio for talking to other aircraft and the tower.
controls.context: The single switches of the radio control box are not described in the sources JoyPro uses.

areas.name: Bomb controls
areas.text: Bomb bay doors, salvo release and fixed guns.

panels.name: Bomb controls
panels.text: Controls for the bomb bay doors, the emergency release of the bombs and the fixed forward guns.
panels.context: Normally the bombardier in the nose aims and drops the bombs; the pilot has these controls too.

controls.name: Bomb bay door lever

positions.name: OPEN
positions.text: The bomb bay doors are open.

positions.name: CLOSED
positions.text: The bomb bay doors are closed.

controls.text: This lever opens and closes the doors of the bomb bay under the fuselage.
controls.context: The doors open before the bomb run and close again afterwards to cut the drag.

controls.name: Bomb salvo release handle
controls.text: Pulling this handle drops all the bombs at once (salvo).
controls.context: It is used in an emergency, to make the aircraft lighter quickly.

controls.name: Fixed gun switches
controls.text: Switches that arm the fixed forward-firing guns in the nose and in the packages on the sides of the fuselage.
controls.context: Gunship versions of the B-25 fired these guns at ground targets from the pilot's wheel.

areas.name: Control wheel and engine levers
areas.text: The wheel and the levers the pilot works.

panels.name: Control wheel
panels.text: The pilot's control column with its wheel, and the gun button on the wheel.
panels.context: The co-pilot has a second column and wheel.

controls.name: Control wheel
controls.text: The column and wheel in front of the pilot. Pushing the column forward lowers the nose, pulling it back raises it; turning the wheel rolls the aircraft to that side, like a car's steering wheel.
controls.context: It is the main flight control; on most bindings it is the joystick's X and Y axes.

controls.name: Gun firing button
controls.text: A button on the pilot's wheel that fires the fixed forward guns.
controls.context: Its exact position on the wheel is not confirmed.

panels.name: Throttle quadrant (engine levers and trims)
panels.text: The paired engine levers on the pedestal (throttles, propeller, mixture and supercharger) and the trim controls.
panels.context: Each pair has one lever per engine; the pilots usually move both together.

controls.name: Left throttle
controls.text: The lever that sets the power of the left engine, read on the manifold pressure gauge.
controls.context: The two throttles are normally moved together; on a HOTAS with one throttle axis both engines can share it.

controls.name: Right throttle
controls.text: The lever that sets the power of the right engine, read on its manifold pressure needle.
controls.context: Setting the two throttles differently helps steer on the ground and balance the engines.

controls.name: Propeller control levers
controls.text: Levers that set how fast the propellers turn (RPM), by changing how sharply the blades bite the air.
controls.context: High RPM is used for take-off and climb, lower RPM for cruise.

controls.name: Mixture control levers
controls.text: Levers that set how much fuel goes into the engines' air (mixture); leaner for high altitudes.
controls.context: Pulling them fully back stops the engines.

controls.name: Supercharger control levers

positions.name: LOW
positions.text: Low blower: for low and medium altitude.

controls.text: Levers that switch the superchargers, pumps that push more air into the engines, between low and high speed (blower).
controls.context: High blower is used at high altitude, where the air is thin.

controls.name: Elevator trim tab wheel
controls.text: A wheel on the left of the pedestal that trims the nose up or down, so the aircraft flies level without the pilot holding the column.
controls.context: The pilot trims after each change of speed, power or load, for example after the bombs are dropped.

controls.name: Aileron and rudder trim knobs
controls.text: Knobs on the pedestal for the aileron trim (keeps the wings level) and the rudder trim; this entry is the aileron trim knob.
controls.context: Aileron trim is needed when the load or the fuel is uneven between the wings.

controls.name: Rudder trim tab control
controls.text: A knob on the pedestal that trims the rudder, so the nose points straight without pressing a pedal.
controls.context: It matters most when one engine fails and the other pulls the nose to one side.
